title: The alternatives
body: jq: jq '. + {total: (.price * .qty)}' works, but jq's syntax is its own language — great once learned, easy to forget between uses. Python: a dict comprehension per row plus file I/O. Fine for a one-off, but it's a script you'll never commit and rewrite next month. Spreadsheet: import, formula, export — and hope the number formatting survives the trip.

title: The Transmute CLI (free)

Given orders.json: [ { "name": "Alice", "price": 10, "qty": 2 }, { "name": "Bob", "price": 5, "qty": 4 } ] $ transmute orders.json \ --pipe '[{"op":"add","fields":{"total":"item.price * item.qty"}}]' \ --output json [ { "name": "Alice", "price": 10, "qty": 2, "total": 20 }, { "name": "Bob", "price": 5, "qty": 4, "total": 20 } ] add works…

title: Gotchas
body: CSV types are inferred. "007" stays a string on purpose (IDs, zip codes); "7" becomes a number. Check edge-case rows once. A failing expression yields null instead of crashing the whole run — handy for messy data, but scan for nulls afterwards ({"op":"filter","expr":"item.total === null"}).

title: PostgreSQL: faster alternative for big files
body: For very large CSVs (100k+ rows) in Postgres, COPY beats row-by-row INSERTs: =# COPY users (id, name, email) FROM '/path/users.csv' CSV HEADER; But COPY needs server-side file access and exact column order. INSERT statements work everywhere — including hosted databases where you only have a SQL editor.

title: SQLite and MySQL notes
body: SQLite: save the output to a file and run sqlite3 mydb.db < inserts.sql. The generated statements use double-quoted identifiers, which SQLite accepts. MySQL: works as-is. If your session has ANSI_QUOTES off and the table name is plain (no reserved words), you can strip the quotes around identifiers without risk.

title: Option 2: Python
body: import csv from xml.etree.ElementTree import Element, tostring root = Element("data") for row in csv.DictReader(open("people.csv", newline="")): item = Element("item") for k, v in row.items(): child = Element(k) child.text = v item.append(child) root.append(item) print(tostring(root, encoding="unicode")) Standard library only — but note it does not escape invalid tag names. A header like first…

title: Things that bite people
body: Tag naming. Column headers become element names: no spaces, can't start with a digit. Rename columns first ({"op":"rename",...}) if needed. Escaping. Values containing & or < must be escaped — always use a serializer. Types. CSV has no types, so everything arrives as text in the XML too. Decide downstream whether <age>32</age> needs casting.

title: Flatten nested JSON arrays
description: Flatten nested JSON arrays and objects into flat CSV rows from the terminal. Free CLI: expand array fields, promote object keys, add computed columns.
body: Updated 7 September 20264 min readCopy link Nested JSON — arrays inside objects inside arrays — is everywhere: API responses, Stripe exports, MongoDB dumps, log files. Spreadsheets can't read it, and most "JSON to CSV" tools either choke on nesting or silently turn your data into [object Object]. This guide shows how to flatten nested JSON into flat rows from the command line, for free, without…

title: Adding computed columns while you're at it
body: The add operation evaluates an expression per row — useful for counts, totals or derived flags: $ transmute items.json -p '[{"op":"add","fields":{"tag_count":"item.tags.length"}}]' -o csv id,name,tags,tag_count 1,Widget,"sale,new",2 2,Gadget,sale,1

title: Deeply nested structures
body: For two or more levels of nesting, chain operations. Flatten level by level: $ transmute orders.json -p '[{"op":"flatten","field":"lines"},{"op":"flatten","field":"discounts"}]' -o csv If a field is missing on some rows, flatten passes those rows through untouched — you don't lose records, they just aren't expanded.

title: Gotchas
body: Arrays of objects: when the flattened values are objects, their keys are merged into the row. Name collisions keep the parent's value unless the child defines the key. null vs missing: both serialize to empty CSV cells; use map if you need to distinguish them. Excel and leading zeros: if IDs like "007" lose their zeros after import, format the column as text in your spreadsheet tool. Huge files:…

title: Getting the CLI
body: MethodCommand npx (no install)npx @mahope/transmute items.json -o csv npm (global)npm i -g @mahope/transmute All processing happens locally. Nothing is uploaded.

title: Flattening nested objects instead of arrays
body: If the nested value is an object rather than an array — say a meta object with several keys — you have two options: Do not leave it nested CSV has no way to hold an object. If a row still contains one when it is serialized, the cell comes out as [object Object], and an array comes out as its elements joined with commas. So promote the fields you need before the CSV step: Promote fields with map…

title: The problem with one-level flattening
body: Take a typical export: [ { "id": 1, "name": "Widget", "tags": ["sale", "new"] }, { "id": 2, "name": "Gadget", "tags": ["sale"] } ] Each item has a tags array. A naive converter gives you a column containing the raw array as text. What you usually want is one row per tag, with the parent fields repeated: $ transmute items.json -p '[{"op":"flatten","field":"tags"}]' -o csv id,name,tags…

title: Gotchas
description: Join two files by a shared key
body: Duplicate keys in the right side: only the last row per key wins — dedupe first if that matters. Type coercion: numeric-looking keys in CSV become numbers on the left but matching is by string, so joins still line up.

title: Compared to the alternatives
description: Join two files by a shared key
body: SQLite: sqlite3 :memory: '.import cart.csv c' ... is powerful but it's five steps of schema wrangling for what is conceptually one lookup. Python/pandas: df.merge() is the right tool at scale; for files under a few MB, startup cost exceeds the whole job. jq: possible with --slurpfile, but the expression syntax for joins is famously hard to get right from memory.

Pasting values by hand doesn't scale, and most online converters want you to upload data you'd rather keep local. Here's the terminal-first path. Option 1: The Transmute CLI (free) Given users.json: [ { "name": "Alice", "age": 32 }, { "name": "Bob",…

title: Loading bigger files
body: A few thousand INSERT lines load fine through any client (psql -f seed.sql). Past tens of thousands of rows, wrap the output in a single transaction so a failure rolls back cleanly instead of leaving half a table: $ { echo 'BEGIN;'; transmute big.json --output sql; echo 'COMMIT;'; } > seed.sql $ psql mydb -f seed.sql

title: Option 1: The Transmute CLI (free)
body: Given users.json: [ { "name": "Alice", "age": 32 }, { "name": "Bob", "age": 25 } ] $ transmute users.json --output sql --table users -- Generated by Transmute INSERT INTO "users" ("name", "age") VALUES ('Alice', 32), ('Bob', 25); The same works for CSV and YAML input — pick the format flag that matches your source: $ transmute people.csv --output sql --table people $ transmute config.yaml…

title: Escaping and types (the part that breaks imports)
body: Quotes are escaped correctly. O'Brien becomes 'O''Brien' — the standard SQL doubling, valid in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite. A string-concatenation approach produces broken statements on exactly this input. Numbers stay numbers. Numeric-looking strings are emitted unquoted so they insert as real numeric columns; everything else is quoted. Nulls are real NULLs. JSON null, missing fields and empty…

title: Shaping rows before they hit the database
body: Because transformation happens before serialization, you filter, sort and reshape in the same command. Only adults, names only: $ transmute users.json --pipe '[{"op":"filter","expr":"item.age > 26"},{"op":"pick","fields":["name"]}]' --output sql --table adults -- Generated by Transmute INSERT INTO "adults" ("name") VALUES ('Alice'); This is where a converter beats a one-off script: the same…

title: Gotchas
body: Column set comes from the union of keys across rows — consistent records convert cleanly, ragged ones get NULLs where fields are missing. Dates stay strings — quote style is correct, but cast to your column type on load if the target isn't text. Reserved words as column names (order, group) are quoted with double quotes, which works in PostgreSQL/SQLite; MySQL needs ANSI_QUOTES mode or backticks.

title: Option 2: Python
body: import json rows = json.load(open("users.json")) cols = list(rows[0]) for row in rows: vals = ", ".join( "NULL" if row.get(c) is None else str(row[c]) if isinstance(row.get(c), (int, float)) else "'" + str(row[c]).replace("'", "''") + "'" for c in cols ) print(f'INSERT INTO users ({", ".join(cols)}) VALUES ({vals});') Zero dependencies — but note what you're signing up for: column inference from…

title: Why not paste it into an online converter?
body: Exports headed for a database often contain customer data, tokens or internal IDs. Uploading them to a random website to get SQL back means trusting a third party with exactly the data you were about to put somewhere permanent. A CLI that runs locally has nowhere to send it.

body: import json from dicttoxml import dicttoxml data = json.load(open("users.json")) print(dicttoxml(data).decode()) pip install dicttoxml. Works, but pulls in more of your dependency tree than most one-off jobs justify.

title: Things that bite people
body: Arrays of objects map naturally; a single bare object needs wrapping first (Transmute does this automatically). Special characters in values must be escaped (&, <). A serializer handles this; string concatenation does not. Nulls: decide whether they become empty elements or disappear — be consistent.

title: XML to JSON
description: Convert XML to JSON from the command line or in code. Free CLI examples you can paste today, plus Python and browser options.
body: Updated 7 September 20262 min readCopy link Legacy APIs, RSS feeds, SOAP responses, Maven and .NET config files — XML is still everywhere, and almost every modern tool wants JSON. Here's how to convert it without hand-writing a parser. Option 1: The Transmute CLI (free) transmute parses XML records into JSON directly. Given this file (users.xml): <data>…

title: Option 3: In your browser
body: For a quick one-off without a terminal, the Transmute desktop app does the same conversion locally; nothing is uploaded.

title: Caveats worth knowing
body: XML has no types. Everything arrives as strings; use a pipeline step like Number(item.age) when you need real numbers. Attributes vs elements. Converters differ on whether <user id="7"> becomes an "id" field. Check the output once before trusting it in bulk. Mixed content (text plus child elements in one node) doesn't map cleanly to JSON in any tool.

title: Option 1: The Transmute CLI (free)
body: transmute parses XML records into JSON directly. Given this file (users.xml): <data> <user><name>Alice</name><age>32</age></user> <user><name>Bob</name><age>25</age></user> </data> run: $ transmute users.xml --format xml --pipe '[{"op":"head","n":10}]' --output json [ { "name": "Alice", "age": "32" }, { "name": "Bob", "age": "25" } ] You can chain operations in the same pass — here filtering and…

title: Option 2: Python
body: import xmltodict, json with open("users.xml") as f: data = xmltodict.parse(f.read()) print(json.dumps(data, indent=2)) pip install xmltodict. Solid, but it's another dependency to pin, and attributes get @-prefixed keys you often have to clean up afterwards.

title: add
description: fields — Add computed columns. Each value is an expression evaluated per row; an expression that throws yields null instead of stopping the run.
body: null {"op":"add","fields":{"total":"item.price * item.qty","vat":"Math.round(item.price * item.qty * 0.25)"}}

title: count
description: Replace the rows with a single {"count": n}. Useful at the end of a filter.
body: {"count": n} {"op":"count"}

title: filter
description: expr — Keep the rows where the expression is true. Strings compare with ===; numbers from CSV are already numbers, values from XML are strings.
body: === {"op":"filter","expr":"item.status === \"shipped\" && item.total > 100"}

title: flatten
description: field — One output row per element of an array field, with the parent's other fields repeated. Object elements are merged into the row; scalar elements land under the field name. Rows without the…
body: {"op":"flatten","field":"items"}

title: group
description: by — One row per distinct value with key, count and the grouped rows under items. Follow with pick to get a plain count table.
body: key count items {"op":"group","by":"city"}, {"op":"pick","fields":["key","count"]}

title: head
description: n — Keep the first n rows (default 10). Good for a quick look at a large file.
body: n {"op":"head","n":5}

title: join
description: on, with, keep, prefix — Merge a second row set on a shared key, compared as strings. Default is an inner join; "keep":"left" keeps unmatched rows. Joined fields can get a prefix so they never…
body: "keep":"left" prefix "with":$(cat other.json) {"op":"join","on":"sku","keep":"left","prefix":"stock_","with":[{"sku":"A1","stock":42}]}

title: map
description: expr — Replace each row with the value of the expression. Wrap object literals in parentheses. For adding a field or two, add is shorter.
body: {"op":"map","expr":"({ id: item.id, name: item.first + ' ' + item.last })"}

title: omit
description: fields — Drop the listed columns and keep everything else.
body: {"op":"omit","fields":["password","internal_note"]}

title: pick
description: fields — Keep only the listed columns, in the order given. Missing fields are skipped rather than filled with null.
body: null {"op":"pick","fields":["id","name","email"]}

title: rename
description: mapping — Rename columns with an old-to-new mapping. Columns not in the mapping keep their names and their position.
body: {"op":"rename","mapping":{"qty":"quantity","cust":"customer"}}

title: sort
description: by, dir — Order by one field. Numbers sort numerically, everything else with locale-aware string comparison. dir is asc (default) or desc; rows missing the field go last.
body: dir asc desc {"op":"sort","by":"total","dir":"desc"}

title: tail
description: n — Keep the last n rows (default 10).

title: unique
description: by — Remove duplicates. With by, the first row per value of that field wins; without it, whole rows are compared.
body: by {"op":"unique","by":"email"}

title: --format, -f
description: json | csv | yaml | xml — Force the input format. Normally detected from the file extension or, for stdin, from the content.
body: $ curl -s https://api.example.com/users | transmute --format json -o csv

title: --help, -h
description: Print the usage text with the same examples as this page.
body: $ transmute --help

title: --output, -o
description: json | csv | yaml | xml | table | sql — The output format. Default is table, an aligned view for the terminal. Redirect with > to write a file.
body: table > $ transmute data.yaml -o json > data.json

title: --pipe, -p
description: — The pipeline as a JSON array. Single-quote it in bash, zsh, Git Bash and WSL. In PowerShell use the stop-parsing token --% and escape inner quotes as \".
body: --% \" $ transmute orders.json --pipe '[{"op":"head","n":3}]'

title: --table
description: — Table name for SQL output (default my_table). Column names come from the keys of all rows combined.
body: my_table $ transmute users.csv -o sql --table users > seed.sql

title: CSV
description: read, write — First line is the header. Values are coerced the way a spreadsheet would: 32 becomes a number, true a boolean, an empty cell an empty string. Quoted fields with commas and doubled…
body: 32 true

title: JSON
description: read, write — An array of objects is the native shape. A single object is treated as one row. Output is pretty-printed with two spaces.

title: SQL
description: write only — One INSERT statement with a row per record. Numbers stay bare, strings are single-quoted with quotes doubled, booleans become TRUE/FALSE, empty and null become NULL. Works as-is in…
body: INSERT TRUE FALSE NULL

title: table
description: write only — An aligned text table for reading in the terminal. It is the default output when no other is given, and not meant to be parsed.

title: XML
description: read, write — Reading: the root's children become rows, child elements become fields, repeated children become arrays. All values are strings, so wrap them in Number() in expressions. Writing: root…
body: Number()

title: YAML
description: read, write — Lists of flat records and simple key–value documents. Not supported: anchors, multi-line strings, deeply nested maps. JSON is valid YAML, so a .yaml file that is really JSON works too.
body: .yaml

title: Can I use the engine from my own code?
body: Yes. require('@mahope/transmute') exposes run(text, inputFormat, pipeline, outputFormat) together with the parsers, serializers and operations. It is one file with no dependencies.

title: Does it work offline?
body: Yes. Neither the CLI nor the desktop app makes a network request. Once installed you can pull the cable out.

title: How do I quote the pipeline on Windows?
body: With difficulty, honestly. In Git Bash or WSL the single-quote form on this page works as written, and that is the recommended route. In PowerShell you can use the stop-parsing token and write inner quotes as \": transmute --% orders.json --pipe "[{\"op\":\"filter\",\"expr\":\"item.status === 'shipped'\"}]" -o csv. That breaks as soon as the pipeline contains < or >, because cmd.exe reads them…

title: What is the difference between the CLI and the desktop app?
body: They share the same engine and produce the same output. The CLI is for scripts, cron jobs, CI and anyone comfortable in a terminal. The desktop app is for building a pipeline interactively and seeing the result while you do it. If you only ever need one, the CLI is the one to start with.

title: What is the licence?
body: The CLI and engine are MIT licensed; the source is on GitHub. The desktop app is a paid product (19 USD one-time) once checkout is live. Until then it is free to download with the limit described above.

title: Where does my data go?
body: Nowhere. Files are read from disk or stdin, transformed in memory and written to stdout. There is no telemetry, no account and no server side.
